briefing.text: The hypothesis has two separable parts: (a) the ARAF variants N217I and G322S are present in iCCA samples, and (b) they lead to pathway activation. A mutation call (genotype) is not a measurement of pathway activity: RAS/RAF mutation status is a poor proxy for MAPK output, which is normally established by readouts such as phospho-MEK/phospho-ERK, a transcriptional output score (e.g. the MPAS genes DUSP4, DUSP6, SPRY2, SPRY4, ETV4, ETV5, PHLDA1, EPHA2, EPHA4, CCND1), drug response, or functional assays of the mutant protein. Before choosing a label: list every column of all five tables and state explicitly whether any column measures pathway output (expression, phospho-protein, RPPA, drug response, functional annotation); write down in advance which observable in these tables would count as supporting the hypothesis and which would count as contradicting it, and check whether either can actually be computed; then say which part of the claim, (a) or (b), your evidence covers. Keep in mind that a non-significant test, a missing variable or a variant seen in a single sample is not by itself a contradicting measurement, and that the hypothesis text is not evidence for itself. Apply the task's label definitions to what you actually find. (The library read the table headers as: patient table = tumour site only; sample table = cancer type, sample type, TMB; plus gene-panel matrix, MAF mutation calls and SV calls. Confirm this yourself; the director has not checked it.)
briefing.reason: The label depends on whether the tables contain anything that measures activation as opposed to mutation presence; the team must make that inventory explicit and separate the two halves of the claim instead of letting variant presence stand in for activation or letting missing evidence stand in for contradiction.

briefing.text: Do not decide that ARAF N217I or G322S is present or absent from a single string match. Protein-change strings depend on the annotated transcript/isoform and on format (HGVSp_Short 'p.N217I' versus HGVSp 'p.Asn217Ile'). Pull ALL rows for ARAF (match by Hugo_Symbol, by Entrez_Gene_Id and by chromosome X coordinates) and print Tumor_Sample_Barcode, HGVSp, HGVSp_Short, Protein_position, Codons and Transcript_ID; also search the whole mutation file for residue numbers 217 and 322. If a variant appears under different numbering, reconcile by codon/genomic coordinate before concluding. Confirm from data_gene_panel_matrix.txt that every sample in the clinical sample table was actually profiled for mutations and for SVs (the library read the matrix as whole-exome for both; verify). Deposited tables for a study sometimes hold only the discovery cohort, so a variant named in a hypothesis may have been found in samples that are not in the deposited table: if a named variant is not found, state that explicitly and reason about whether that is absence of the key variable or evidence about the claim, rather than assuming either.
briefing.reason: Whether the two named variants can be located in the mutation table is the first fact everything else rests on, and a format or isoform mismatch, or an unprofiled sample, would give a wrong presence/absence call.

briefing.text: Do not infer that an ARAF missense change is activating from its position in the protein, residue conservation, or analogy to BRAF V600E. RAF-family missense mutants fall into different functional classes: RAS-independent activating mutants (signalling as monomers or dimers), kinase-impaired or kinase-dead mutants that raise ERK signalling only through RAS and wild-type CRAF, and neutral passengers. Which class a variant belongs to has been established by in-vitro kinase assays and phospho-ERK measurements in cells, not from sequence. Check whether the mutation table has any functional-effect or oncogenic-effect column (the library's reading of the header found Consequence, Variant_Classification, HGVSp, Hotspot and Annotation_Status, and no functional-effect field; verify, and look at what the Hotspot column actually contains for the ARAF rows). If there is no such column, describe the variant's location as context only, not as evidence of activation.
briefing.reason: Prevents the team from treating domain location or a consequence annotation as a stand-in for functional evidence of gain-of-function, which would change what they count as support.

briefing.text: If you examine co-occurring alterations, build a per-sample table of all alterations in RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK genes and upstream receptor-tyrosine-kinase genes (also NF1) for ARAF-variant carriers and non-carriers, using BOTH data_mutations.txt and data_sv.txt, because fusions are recorded only in the SV file. Interpret with care in both directions: kinase-impaired RAF mutants depend on and tend to co-occur with upstream RAS activation, so a co-occurring driver does not refute a role for the ARAF variant, and the absence of another driver does not prove one. If a carrier also has a canonical pathway driver, activation cannot be assigned to the ARAF variant from these data; if it has none, record that as 'consistent with' only.
briefing.reason: A co-alteration analysis is the most likely indirect argument the team will attempt; they need to include the SV file and to know that neither co-occurrence nor its absence is decisive.

briefing.text: Mutual exclusivity between ARAF variants and known pathway drivers (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, receptor-kinase fusions) cannot serve as proof of shared pathway activation in a cohort of only a handful of samples. Pairwise/Fisher tests assume identically distributed samples and are confounded by tumour mutation burden and subtype, and with fewer than about 10 samples and 1-2 carriers the smallest attainable p-value is usually above 0.05, so the test cannot be informative either way. Count the samples (clinical sample table) and the carriers, compute the minimum attainable Fisher p-value given the margins, and compare TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS of carriers and non-carriers. If the test is underpowered, report the co-alteration pattern descriptively only: do not call exclusivity 'support' for activation and do not call a non-significant result 'contradiction'.
briefing.reason: The data files are tiny (sample table about 1 kB), so any exclusivity or association test is likely underpowered; the team should check power before reading anything into a p-value.

briefing.text: Do not argue driver status for the ARAF variants from allele fraction or from mere presence without checking passenger likelihood. VAF reflects purity, copy number and clonality together; ARAF is on chromosome X, so it is hemizygous in male tumours and expected VAFs differ by sex (the library reports the patient table has no sex column; verify). Check whether t_ref_count/t_alt_count are populated at all (the library saw them empty in the first data row of the MAF; verify across all rows); if they are empty, make no clonality or driver claim from VAF. Compare each carrier's TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS and total mutation count with the rest of the cohort: if a carrier is among the most heavily mutated samples, the ARAF variant is more plausibly a passenger and confidence should be lowered accordingly.
briefing.reason: Stops an unsupported VAF/clonality argument and adds a concrete passenger-likelihood check (carrier mutation burden versus cohort) that affects how much weight variant presence can carry.

shared_assumptions: Both teams fixed a decision rule before looking at values in which the label depends only on whether a pathway-output column exists in the headers. Once no such column was found, nothing computed from the rows (presence of the two named variants, recurrence, co-alteration pattern) could move the label. Neither team tested whether that rule is the only reasonable application of the task's three label definitions to a two-part claim whose first part (the two named ARAF variants occur in iCCA) is measured and confirmed.
Both teams took 'the pathway' to mean the MAPK/ERK cascade; the hypothesis text does not name it.

Both teams treated the absence of SV rows for a sample as 'no fusion detected'. Team B stated this outright; team A relied on the gene panel matrix listing all 8 samples as WXS for structural variants. Every SV row is RNA-supported and not DNA-supported, and two samples (ICC18, an ARAF carrier, and ICC22) have no rows, so 'not assayed by RNA' was not ruled out.

Both teams treated the mutation table as a complete exome call set when stating that no sample has a KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutation and that neither ARAF carrier has a competing driver. All 218 rows are SNPs (no indel at all) and no IDH1/IDH2/KRAS/TP53/BAP1 call exists in any of the 8 tumours, so the call set may be filtered or of limited sensitivity.

Both teams cite Hotspot = 0 for the two ARAF rows as part of 'no functional annotation'. The column is constant (0 in all 212 annotated rows), so there is no positive control showing it can ever be non-zero in this file.
unused_evidence: data_sv.txt columns DNA_support / RNA_support: all 15 rows are DNA_support=No, RNA_support=Yes. This shows RNA sequencing was done on at least 6 of the 8 tumours although no expression table is supplied, and it contradicts the panel matrix label 'WXS' for structural variants. Neither team mentioned these columns.

RIN1 fusion rows in data_sv.txt: RIN1-IGLL5 in ICC12 (the G322S carrier) and RIN1-IGLJ3 in ICC14 and ICC8. RIN1 is a RAS-binding protein; neither team's pathway gene list (RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK/RTK/NF1/FGFR) appears to include it, and neither team commented on a 3-of-8 recurrent event with immunoglobulin-lambda partners.
Variant_Type (SNP only) and the absence of any canonical iCCA driver call in the MAF, as an indicator of how complete the call set is.

dbSNP_RS (populated for 66 of 218 rows; empty for both ARAF rows) together with the entirely empty Matched_Norm and Mutation_Status columns: somatic status of the calls cannot be confirmed from the table, and neither team used dbSNP_RS to gauge germline leakage.
Gene-level recurrence against a length-scaled background: team B counted recurrent genes (ARAF, MUC16, ACAN) but did not scale by gene length; team A did not run a recurrence analysis at all.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: weakest point is the choice between 'Not verifiable' and 'True' (confidence 0.6). Reported, not resolved: no check was run that could have discriminated between the two readings.

Team B: the same weakest point in nearly the same words (confidence 0.6), also only reported. Team B's pitfalls_checked list is empty, and its statement 'missing SV rows mean no fusion detected' was asserted without a check.
second_readings: Reading 1 (both teams): the claim is a functional one, 'these variants activate the pathway', and needs a pathway-activity measurement, which the tables lack.

Reading 2: the claim is compound, '(a) ARAF N217I and G322S occur in iCCA and (b) they activate the pathway'. Part (a) is measured and holds at the exact residues named. The task's 'Not verifiable' definition speaks of data holding 'no relevant variables or tables'; the mutation table is a relevant table for part (a). Whether a confirmed part (a) plus an unmeasured part (b) is 'support' or 'cannot be settled' is the open point.
Reading 3: 'the pathway' is unnamed. If a team reads it as anything other than MAPK/ERK, the gene list used for the co-alteration table changes.
'in iCCA': all 8 samples are intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma primaries, so the population is not in doubt.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust. The agreed label follows from a defensible reading of the task's definitions (no table measures pathway activity), but it rests on that reading alone: both teams named the same True-versus-Not-verifiable judgement as their weakest point at confidence 0.6 and neither ran a check that could separate the readings. Their supporting context ('no competing driver in either carrier') also leans on untested assumptions about SV and mutation call-set completeness, though I see nothing in the tables that would by itself overturn the label.

questions.why: Both teams cite a zero hotspot flag on the variants of interest as absence of functional annotation. If the column is a default that is never filled for this kind of file, it is not evidence of anything and must not be read as a neutral annotation.

findings.question: In cBioPortal-format mutation files annotated through the Genome Nexus pipeline, how is the 'Hotspot' column populated: which hotspot resource is consulted, does a value of 0 mean the variant was looked up and is not a known hotspot, and are there known circumstances in which the column is 0 for every row regardless of the variant?
findings.answer: The 'Hotspot' column in the file is not a looked-up annotation, so 0 does not mean 'checked and not a hotspot'. cBioPortal's hotspot calls come from cancerhotspots.org (recurrent linear hotspots) and 3dhotspots.org, but they are applied on the fly through Genome Nexus when the portal displays a variant; they are not written into the data file. The Genome Nexus annotation pipeline's documented output fields (gene, coordinates, HGVSc/HGVSp/HGVSp_Short, Transcript_ID, RefSeq, Protein_position, Codons, Exon_Number, optional gnomAD/SIFT/PolyPhen/MutationAssessor/OncoKB columns, Annotation_Status) include no Hotspot field, and the cBioPortal MAF format documentation defines no Hotspot column. Yes, there is a known all-zero circumstance: a user on the cBioPortal forum reported that in downloaded study files the hotspot column 'only contains zeros (even for positive hits like BRAF V600E)' across several versions of TCGA studies; the cBioPortal developer who replied did not dispute it and said hotspots are annotated on the fly and must be fetched from the Genome Nexus API. The column should therefore be treated as a placeholder. A zero on the variants of interest is not evidence of absent functional annotation and not a neutral annotation either. Simple check for the teams: if no row in the whole file is non-zero, the column carries no information. Limit: no documentation page states the default in words; the conclusion rests on the pipeline's field list plus the forum report.

findings.question: In the cBioPortal structural-variant file format, what do the DNA_support and RNA_support fields mean, and when the gene panel matrix marks a sample as profiled for structural variants but the sample has no rows in the SV file, does the convention treat it as 'profiled with no event found' or can it mean the sample was not assayed by the RNA-based method?
findings.answer: DNA_support and RNA_support are optional yes/no flags supplied by the data provider. DNA_support = 'Fusion detected from DNA sequence data'; RNA_support = 'Fusion detected from RNA sequence data' (the current SV column table repeats the word DNA in the RNA_Support row, a documentation typo; the legacy fusion-format section says RNA). They describe the evidence type for a row that exists and say nothing about samples without rows. The gene panel matrix exists because, in the documentation's words, the MAF and structural variant formats 'are unable to include samples which are sequenced but contain no called mutations'; a panel name in a sample's structural_variants cell means profiled, NA means not profiled. So the portal convention is 'profiled, no event reported'. However, the matrix holds one panel name per sample per profile and cannot record which assay (DNA exome or RNA-seq) was run on which sample. If the SV rows are RNA-supported only while the panel named is a DNA assay such as WXS, the files cannot show that the samples without rows had RNA sequenced. In that situation a missing fusion row is an unverified negative for RNA-detected fusions, not an observed negative. The documentation does not address mixed DNA/RNA assays directly, so this last step is a reading of the format's limits, not a stated rule. Confidence split: high for the field definitions and the matrix convention, medium for whether a sample without rows was RNA-assayed.

findings.question: What is the role of the RIN1 protein in RAS signalling, and are chimeric transcripts joining an expressed gene to immunoglobulin lambda segments (IGLL5, IGLJ) a recognised artefact of RNA-seq fusion callers, for example from plasma-cell infiltration or read-through mapping?
findings.answer: RIN1: a RAS effector that binds GTP-loaded RAS with affinity similar to RAF1 (Kd about 22 nM) and competes directly with RAF1 for RAS. Unlike other effectors it inhibits transformation by activated RAS (about twofold fewer soft-agar colonies, more when membrane-targeted) and is restrained by 14-3-3 binding at Ser351, a PKD site. Search summaries that I did not open add that it is a RAB5 exchange factor promoting EGFR endocytosis and an ABL kinase activator. RIN1 is thus a negative modulator of the RAS-RAF branch, not a MAPK activator. No page I read describes RIN1 fusions as a known MAPK-activating event; arguing that a RIN1 fusion raises RAF signalling would be speculation. Immunoglobulin partners: the web only partly settles this. The general artefact class is established: very high expression of one partner produces non-specific chimeras through reverse-transcriptase template switching during cDNA preparation, and fusions recurring at improbable frequency are filtered as false positives (Stransky 2014). A myeloma fusion study pooled IGLL5 into the IGL locus, removed 18 highly recurrent IGL fusions for low whole-genome support, filtered promiscuous partners, and states that transcript overexpression makes false-positive chimeric transcripts more likely (Foltz 2020). Not settled: no page I read says specifically that IGLL5/IGLJ chimeras in solid tumours arise from plasma-cell infiltration or read-through mapping; that mechanism is plausible but unconfirmed here, and the Arriba documentation could not be retrieved. Practical reading: a gene-IGLL5/IGLJ call with RNA support only, no DNA support, and the same Ig partner recurring across samples is a probable artefact or at best an unknown. It should not be counted as a pathway alteration, and it does not by itself confirm 'no other pathway alteration' either. Confidence split: high for RIN1 function, medium for the immunoglobulin artefact question.
